title: Introducing Alternate Clouds: Decentralized Infrastructure for Services and Agent Swarms
excerpt: Alternate Clouds gives teams one web and CLI workflow for deploying application services and coordinated AI agent swarms on decentralized infrastructure.
content: Cloud platforms made deployment easier, but they also concentrated applications, billing, and operational control inside a small number of vendors. Distributed compute creates more infrastructure choice, yet raw capacity alone does not give a team a usable product experience.
**Alternate Clouds is the deployment platform from Alternate Futures.** It brings application services and coordinated AI agent swarms into one project-centered workflow.
## Why decentralized infrastructure?

A useful decentralized cloud should make infrastructure choices visible without requiring every developer to become an infrastructure operator. Teams should be able to select resources, regions, and workload controls while the platform handles deployment state, health, logs, access, and billing.
The goal is practical control:
- **Infrastructure choice** -- deploy workloads across independent compute providers
- **Workload portability** -- describe the service instead of rebuilding it around one vendor
- **Operational visibility** -- keep deployments, logs, health, networking, and spend in one place
- **Guarded autonomy** -- give agent teams models and tools through explicit policy and budget controls
## What ships in open beta
Alternate Clouds supports several workload paths through the same service model:
| Workload | Deployment path |
| Application services | Templates, GitHub repositories, Docker images, functions, or empty servers |
| GPU workloads | Services configured with explicit compute, GPU, and region requirements |
| Confidential services | Workloads placed on confidential compute when the service requires it |
| Agent swarms | Multi-agent teams with sequential, parallel, loop, supervisor, handoff, or graph topologies |

Every service lives inside a project and uses the same core operational surfaces. Swarms add a Source editor for agents and topology, version history, a private chat room, optional Discord channels, and per-run inference cost visibility.
## One platform, two paths
The web app starts with **New Service**. Choose a service type, configure its source and resources, then deploy from the shared service workspace.
The CLI exposes the same service workflow:
```bash
npm install -g @alternatefutures/acc
acc login
acc projects create --name my-project
acc services create
acc services deploy
For a swarm, the workflow adds local authoring and testing before the cloud deployment:
```bash
acc swarms init my-swarm && cd my-swarm
acc add agent
acc add swarm
acc run review --input "Say hello in one sentence."
acc swarms deploy review --yes
acc run review --remote --input "Say hello in one sentence."

By default, local and deployed swarms call supported models through the platform and charge usage to the organization. A team does not need to paste a model-provider secret to complete the standard flow.
## Why swarms matter

A single agent can handle a bounded task. A swarm can divide work among named agents, run them in a defined topology, and preserve a visible record of who ran, what it cost, and whether the run succeeded. That makes multi-agent work something a team can operate rather than a collection of prompts held together by convention.
Deployed swarms can answer in their private end-to-end-encrypted room or in connected Discord channels. Tools remain off by default and are granted through reviewed policy.
## Open beta
Alternate Clouds is now in open beta. [Join the open beta](https://www.alternatefutures.ai) to deploy a service or build your first agent team.
The decentralized cloud becomes useful when deploying and operating on it feels ordinary.

title: How to Deploy Your First AI Agent Swarm on Alternate Clouds
excerpt: Create an agent team, test it locally, deploy it to decentralized compute, and run it through the Alternate Clouds CLI.
content: Alternate Clouds lets you define a team of named agents, choose how they work together, test the team locally, and deploy the same swarm to decentralized compute. This guide follows the production-proven open-beta workflow.
> The standard path does not require a model-provider secret. Local and deployed runs use the platform's inference service and charge usage to your organization. Bringing your own key is optional.
## Prerequisites
- An Alternate Futures account
- The current Alternate Clouds CLI
- An organization with enough wallet balance for inference and the deployment lease
## 1. Install and sign in
```bash
npm install -g @alternatefutures/acc
cd ~ && acc login
acc whoami
The login command opens a browser for approval. The final command confirms which account the CLI will use.
## 2. Create a project
```bash
cd ~ && acc projects create --name my-swarm-project
You can switch between existing projects later with `acc projects switch`. Every swarm command uses the active project unless you pass `--project` explicitly.
## 3. Initialize the swarm
```bash
cd ~
acc swarms init my-swarm
cd my-swarm
This creates `swarm.toml` and the project folders used for agent definitions and personas.
## 4. Add an agent and a team
```bash
acc add agent
acc add swarm

The first wizard asks for the agent's one-word name, job, and model. The second asks for a team name, topology, and members. Choose the sequential topology for a simple first run. In the examples below, the agent is named `researcher` and the team is named `review`.
Supported topologies include sequential, parallel with a reducer, loop, supervisor, handoff, and custom graph connections.
## 5. Test locally
```bash
acc run review --input "Say hello in one sentence."
The swarm runtime executes on your machine while the model request goes through Alternate Clouds. Use `acc dev` when you want the local inspector and model diagnostics.
## 6. Deploy
```bash
acc swarms deploy review --yes
acc swarms status review

The platform compiles the saved definition, resolves the released runtime, creates the runtime secrets and policy material, reserves compute capacity, and waits for the runtime to register. The swarm is ready when status reports `ACTIVE` and `runtime_ready: true`.

Only one deployment of a swarm can run at a time. An unchanged deploy reports `Nothing changed`; after changing the model, definition, or channel map, stop the existing deployment before deploying again.
## 7. Run it in the cloud
```bash
acc run review --remote --input "Draft a short launch checklist."
A successful run returns the answer, run identifier, and cost. The cost combines model usage and the deployment lease; runs also appear in the service's inference spend view.
## 8. Join the private room
```bash
acc swarms room review
acc chat join chat.alternatefutures.ai

The first command prints the room's six-word passphrase. Inside the room, `@researcher` addresses one agent and `@all` runs the whole swarm. A message without a mention runs nothing and costs nothing.
Every deployed swarm gets one private end-to-end-encrypted room. The bridge that speaks for the agents runs inside the swarm deployment and is scoped to that swarm.
## 9. Operate and stop
```bash
acc swarms logs review --tail 200
acc swarms stop review
Tools are off by default and must be granted through reviewed policy. Stopping the swarm closes its lease and stops the compute charge.
## Web app path

The same workflow is available without installing the CLI: create or open a project, choose **New Service > Swarm**, add the agents and topology on **Source**, save the definition, and deploy from the footer. The Source tab also manages the private room, Discord connections, and version history.

title: The Web3 Infrastructure Gap: Why Decentralized Compute Needs an Application Layer
excerpt: Decentralized compute has capacity. What application teams still need is a usable layer for deploying services and operating AI agent swarms.
content: Decentralized infrastructure has spent years proving that independent providers can supply storage, CPUs, GPUs, and confidential compute. The harder product problem now sits one layer higher: how does an application team use that capacity without assembling its own cloud platform?
## The gap is operational
Teams that want alternatives to a single cloud vendor still face three incomplete choices:
- **Centralized application platforms** provide a polished workflow but keep deployment, billing, and availability inside one vendor
- **Raw compute marketplaces** provide capacity but leave service configuration, secrets, networking, health, logs, and lifecycle management to the customer
- **Agent frameworks** help define behavior but usually stop before deployment, model billing, policy, recovery, and multi-agent operations
The missing layer is not another marketplace. It is an application platform that turns distributed capacity into services a team can deploy and operate.
## AI raises the bar

AI workloads make the application layer more important. A production agent may need a model, durable state, a tool policy, an execution budget, a private place to receive work, and an audit trail. A multi-agent swarm adds topology, versioning, per-agent identity, coordination, and per-run cost.
Raw infrastructure does not provide those product-level controls by itself.
> Decentralized compute becomes useful to application teams when the operational experience is as coherent as the infrastructure beneath it is distributed.
## What the application layer should provide
Alternate Clouds brings the current product surface into one project and service model.
### For application services
- Create services from templates, GitHub repositories, Docker images, functions, or empty servers
- Choose compute, storage, GPU, region, budget, and runtime controls
- Inspect deployment state, health, logs, networking, and spend from one workspace
- Use the web app for guided setup or the `acc` CLI for repeatable workflows
### For agent swarms
- Define named agents and choose how they work together
- Test the same team locally before deploying it to the cloud
- Run sequential, parallel, loop, supervisor, handoff, or graph topologies
- Give each deployed swarm a private encrypted room and optional Discord channels
- Track model usage, lease cost, run status, and service spend
- Keep tools off by default and grant them through explicit policy
### For operators
- Manage services and swarms inside the same project model
- Route model calls through the platform by default or bring an organization or project key
- Stop a workload to close its lease and end the compute charge
- Keep the provider-specific mechanics behind a consistent deployment surface
## What decentralized should mean

Decentralization is not a badge. It changes where workloads run, how capacity is selected, what can fail, and how recovery works. Those choices should be visible to the operator without becoming the developer's full-time job.
That is the application-layer opportunity: preserve infrastructure choice while making deployment, policy, communication, and cost legible.
## The open-beta test

Alternate Clouds is testing that proposition now with application services and deployable agent swarms. A user can build a team in the web app or CLI, run it locally, deploy it, talk to it in a private room, connect a Discord channel, inspect cost, and stop the lease from the same platform.
[Join the open beta](https://www.alternatefutures.ai) and tell us where the application layer still gets in your way.
